mcq.q: In Fisher's equation MV = PT, the money supply is ₹500 crore, velocity is 4 and the volume of transactions is 1,000 crore units. The price level is:
mcq.explain: From MV = PT, P = MV ÷ T = (500 × 4) ÷ 1,000 = 2,000 ÷ 1,000 = 2. Fisher's quantity theory assumes V and T are constant in the short run, so the price level changes in proportion to the money supply.
mcq.topic: Classical approach — Fisher's quantity theory (MV = PT)

mcq.q: According to Fisher's quantity theory, if the money supply doubles while V and T are constant, the price level will:
mcq.explain: With V and T held constant, MV = PT means that P changes in the same proportion as M. If M doubles, P doubles and the value of money is halved. This proportional relationship is the core of the classical quantity theory of money.
mcq.topic: Classical approach — Fisher's quantity theory (MV = PT)
mcq.fast: V, T fixed -> P moves one-for-one with M.

mcq.q: In the Cambridge equation Md = kPY, k = 0.25 and nominal income PY = ₹4,000 crore. The demand for money is:
mcq.explain: Md = k × PY = 0.25 × 4,000 = ₹1,000 crore. Here k is the proportion of nominal income people wish to hold as cash balances; it is the reciprocal of the income velocity of money (velocity = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4). Dividing by k instead of multiplying gives ₹16,000 crore.

mcq.q: Nominal GDP is ₹3,000 lakh crore and the money supply is ₹600 lakh crore. The income velocity of money is:
mcq.explain: Income velocity of money = nominal income ÷ money supply = 3,000 ÷ 600 = 5. On average, each rupee changes hands five times in the year in buying final goods and services. In the Cambridge version, k = 1 ÷ V = 0.2.
mcq.topic: Classical approach — Fisher's quantity theory (MV = PT)

mcq.q: Under the Baumol inventory approach, the optimal size of each conversion of bonds into cash is √(2bY/r). If the brokerage cost per conversion b = ₹10, income Y = ₹2,000 and the interest rate r = 0.04, the optimal size of each conversion is:
mcq.explain: Optimal conversion = √(2 × 10 × 2,000 ÷ 0.04) = √(40,000 ÷ 0.04) = √10,00,000 = ₹1,000, so the average cash held would be half of this. The formula shows that money demand rises with income and brokerage cost but falls as the interest rate rises, though less than proportionately (the square-root rule).

mcq.q: In Keynes's theory, how does the speculative demand for money move with the interest rate?
options: Inversely related to the rate of interest
Directly related to the rate of interest
Independent of the rate of interest
mcq.explain: People hold money for speculation when they expect bond prices to fall (interest rates to rise). When the interest rate is high, people expect it to fall and bond prices to rise, so they prefer bonds and hold little speculative money. When the rate is low, they hold more money. Hence an inverse relationship.
mcq.topic: Keynes's liquidity preference theory — three motives
mcq.fast: Speculative Md: high interest -> hold bonds, low money.

options: Monetary policy becomes ineffective, as extra money is simply held at a very low interest rate
People refuse to hold any money
The demand for money is perfectly inelastic
mcq.explain: At a very low interest rate, everyone expects rates to rise and bond prices to fall, so people are willing to hold any extra money instead of buying bonds. The demand for money becomes perfectly elastic, and increases in the money supply cannot lower the interest rate further. Monetary policy loses its power.
mcq.fast: Liquidity trap = very low rate + perfectly elastic Md + monetary policy useless.

mcq.q: A loan taken today is to be repaid in money after two years. Here money is serving as a:
mcq.explain: Money serves as a standard of deferred payments when future payments, such as loan repayments, salaries due or instalments, are expressed in money. Its other functions are medium of exchange, unit of account (measure of value) and store of value.
mcq.topic: Introduction — money, its functions and characteristics
mcq.fast: Future payment in money = standard of deferred payments.

mcq.q: Milton Friedman treated the demand for money as depending mainly on:
options: Permanent income and the returns on other assets
mcq.explain: In his restatement of the quantity theory, Friedman treated money as one of several assets in which wealth can be held. The demand for money depends on permanent income (a measure of wealth), the expected returns on bonds, equities and goods, and inflation. He found money demand to be fairly stable.
mcq.topic: Friedman's restatement of the quantity theory
mcq.fast: Friedman = money as an asset; permanent income.
